Te Linde’s Operative Gynecology · Chapter 24

Laparoscopic Hysterectomy

Minimally Invasive Hysterectomy — Ted L. Anderson & Ronald D. Alvarez
Robotic-assisted hysterectomy is excluded throughout, as requested. Content drawn from the chapter text; figures extracted from the source PDF.

“Minimally invasive hysterectomy” is a family of procedures that differ in how much of the operation is done laparoscopically — and the choice among them is driven by pathology and surgeon capability rather than by the instrument.

1989First laparoscopic hysterectomy described
40%Benign hysterectomies done laparoscopically by 2010
~100Cases before complication rates plateau
0.12–0.34Deaths per 1000 hysterectomies, any route
Starting point

The commonest gynecologic operation

Hysterectomy is the most common gynecologic procedure performed worldwide, and historically most were done through a laparotomy incision.

Shift

Laparoscopic became the majority

By 2010, 40% of hysterectomies for benign indications were laparoscopic, with growing use for selected gynecologic cancers. By 2020, most were performed laparoscopically.

Guidance

Societies favour minimally invasive

ACOG and AAGL both encourage a minimally invasive approach to hysterectomy — a recommendation that explicitly includes the vaginal route.

Two operations here

TLH and LSH

Total laparoscopic hysterectomy completes the entire procedure laparoscopically including cuff closure. Laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy leaves the cervix.

Principle

The decision on whether hysterectomy is the right therapeutic intervention is the same regardless of route. What the laparoscopic question decides is only the method of access — and that is largely a function of patient pathology and surgeon skill.

On the vaginal route

The eVALuate trial concluded TLH gave less pain, quicker recovery and better quality of life than abdominal hysterectomy — but also that TVH was the preferred approach, offering similar benefits at less cost and with shorter operating times.

How laparoscopic hysterectomy arrived

Laparoscopy entered gynecologic practice in the 1950s through Raoul Palmer in France, followed by Kurt Semm in Germany. The landmark description of the first laparoscopic hysterectomy came in 1989 from Harry Reich and John DeCaprio, who framed it as a substitute for abdominal hysterectomy rather than for vaginal hysterectomy — an approach that might avoid the morbidity of abdominal surgery while keeping thorough visualisation and easy access to the vascular pedicles.

And how supracervical hysterectomy came back

Supracervical hysterectomy was first performed by Wilhelm Alexander Freund in 1878 and led practice for over 80 years. Removing the cervix then carried peritonitis, fistula, haemorrhage, ureteral injury, cystotomy and enterotomy; through the 1930s mortality for total hysterectomy ran 50% higher than for the supracervical operation. By the late 1940s it was abandoned in favour of total hysterectomy, reflecting better instruments, safer antibiotics, improved blood banking, and recognition of cervical cancer developing in almost 2% of patients with residual cervices.

Interest returned in the early 1990s after Kurt Semm and Thomas Lyons described laparoscopic techniques for it — driven partly by the operation being easier, quicker and safer to perform than TLH, and partly by instrument refinement.

Three structures decide the safety of the operation: the ureter on the pelvic sidewall, the bladder over the lower segment, and the ascending uterine vessels in the broad ligament.

Finding the ureter without dissecting for it

  • Laparoscopically the ureter can usually be seen through intact peritoneum, crossing the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the external and internal iliac vessels.
  • It then courses across the pelvic sidewall inferior to the infundibulopelvic ligament but superior to the uterosacral ligament.
  • Where that is the case, retroperitoneal dissection adds no benefit at this point and may cause unnecessary bleeding.
  • In distorted anatomy the traditional approach is preferred: incise the round ligament, enter the retroperitoneum, identify the ureter and follow its course toward the uterine artery before isolating the adnexa.
Pearl

Keeping the ureter in view rather than dissecting it out is the laparoscopic advantage here — magnification and the transperitoneal view substitute for the retroperitoneal exposure an open operation would need.

The broad ligament and the bladder flap

The plane

  • Once the round ligament is divided, the anterior and posterior leaves of the broad ligament separate easily.
  • Dissection continues in this avascular plane toward the junction of cervix and corpus.
  • Transecting the anterior leaf across the cervix develops the bladder flap.
  • Loose areolar tissue between the leaves is teased away bluntly or sharply to reveal the uterine vessels on the lateral aspect of the uterus.
Energy discipline

Use cold sharp dissection when developing the bladder flap — or only very brief pulses of bipolar current for superficial peritoneal vessels — until the anatomic limits of the bladder are defined.

The adnexal pedicles

  • After the corpus is out, access to the adnexa is unobstructed and the infundibulopelvic ligament is easily distinguished from the ureter.
  • Retract the adnexa medially from the ipsilateral side while sealing and transecting the pedicle from the contralateral side.
  • That geometry applies the energy source perpendicular to the pedicle, which maximises instrument performance and minimises collateral thermal damage.
When the order has to be reversed

Where an ovarian or uterine neoplasm makes it preferable to remove the uterus intact with the adnexal structures attached, the steps are reversed: identify the ureter retro- or transperitoneally, coagulate and transect the infundibulopelvic ligament, then transect the round ligament.

What the colpotomy ring defines anatomically

When the ring is placed and identified appropriately, the level of cervical amputation is at the cardinal ligament. So when the posterior colpotomy incision is made, the uterosacral ligaments remain attached to the fascia of the vaginal apex — which is what makes incorporating them into the cuff closure possible. The ring also lateralises and protects the ureters and identifies the vaginal fornices.

The family runs from an entirely vaginal operation to one done completely through the ports, and the dividing line that matters most clinically is whether the cervix comes out.

Classification explorer

The minimally invasive hysterectomy family

Select a procedure for its definition, evidence base and the patients it suits.

The five components of the operation

Component 1

Separation of the adnexal structures from the uterine corpus for preservation, or from the abdominal wall for subsequent removal.

Component 2

Dissecting, occluding and dividing the blood supply before extirpating the uterine corpus.

Component 3

Transection of the cardinal ligament complex with colpotomy and amputation of the cervix from the vaginal apex. For LSH this instead becomes amputation of the corpus from the cervix above the cardinal ligament.

Component 4

Removing the specimen. For LSH the options here are fewer.

Component 5

Closing the vaginal cuff, with or without colposuspension. Not needed for LSH.

Components 1 and 2 are identical between TLH and LSH.

Pearl

For a very large fibroid uterus, or significantly distorted benign anatomy, it can help to perform an LSH first — in the absence of endometrial neoplasm — and then address the colpotomy and cervical amputation with the corpus out of the operative field.

Indication, not preference

Supracervical hysterectomy is indicated for selected patients who choose it after appropriate counselling, and occasionally in surgical emergencies. It should not be performed simply because the surgeon is uncomfortable removing the cervix — in that situation, assistance from a more skilled surgeon should be sought.

Why the cancer-prevention argument for removing the cervix has weakened

The rationale for routine cervical removal to prevent cervical cancer has been largely eliminated by the effectiveness of present-day precancer screening and improved treatment of preinvasive disease. Cervical dysplasia is rare in appropriately selected low-risk patients, and there is no evidence that supracervical hysterectomy increases the risk of cervical cancer. Removal of the corpus alone is adequate treatment for abnormal uterine bleeding or benign uterine fibroids.

A 2-year prospective study showed overall improvement in sexual functioning after TLH — increased libido, coital activity and orgasm with decreased dyspareunia. Several studies suggesting increased orgasmic frequency after LSH were not confirmed by subsequent work. Perception nonetheless remains a powerful motivator, and many women considering elective hysterectomy treat cervical preservation as pivotal.

Patient evaluation, selection and optimisation are identical whatever laparoscopic procedure is planned — the patient has to be a candidate for surgery, then for hysterectomy, then for laparoscopy.

Contraindications to laparoscopic hysterectomy
CategoryExamples
Limits on pneumoperitoneum, ventilation or Trendelenburg positioningMorbid obesity; increased intracranial pressure; ventriculoperitoneal shunt; portal or pulmonary hypertension
Conditions precluding safe entry or adequate operating spaceSevere abdominal or pelvic adhesive disease; advanced pregnancy; bulky uterine or fibroid size preventing access to the uterine vessels

There are few contraindications, and most are relative — related to comorbidities, deficiencies in main physiologic functions, and elevated body mass index.

Preparation

Comorbidities

Optimise before the list

Diabetes, hypertension and pulmonary compromise should be evaluated and optimised before any elective intervention.

Anesthesia liaison

Insufflation plus Trendelenburg

Coordinate on the effect of abdominal insufflation and prolonged Trendelenburg on peak inspiratory pressures and cardiac preload.

Consent

Include conversion

Discuss the possibility of not completing laparoscopically — poor tolerance of positioning, equipment malfunction — and the potential need to convert to laparotomy.

Consent

Include tissue removal

Risks and benefits of energy-based instruments and morcellators belong in the consent, along with alternatives such as vaginal morcellation or laparotomy.

Positioning

  • Low lithotomy, giving access to the perineum for uterine manipulation and tissue removal.
  • The patient must be far enough down the table — a concept often underestimated, and one that shows up later as the table blocking the manipulator's range of motion mid-procedure.
  • Rocking the hips forward reduces lordosis and stabilises the pelvis.
  • Arm and leg position and padding must relieve pressure points that could cause nerve injury.
  • A draw sheet across the table, wrapped under well-padded arms and tucked back under the patient, stabilises the arms, keeps IVs and the blood pressure cuff working, and leaves the surgeon mobile.
Principle

Before scrubbing, place the patient in maximum Trendelenburg to confirm stability — the tilt test. It also lets the anesthesiologist assess pulmonary status in steep Trendelenburg. She is then returned level.

Shoulder braces

Braces are discouraged because of the increased potential for brachial plexus injury. Where they are used, placing them laterally over the acromioclavicular joint rather than medially on the shoulder may minimise that risk.

Stopping the patient sliding

Place the patient directly on a foam pad taped to the operating table, or another pad designed to prevent slippage; a gel pad or surgical beanbag can stabilise larger patients. A foam pad and straps across the chest, secured to the bed with tape or Velcro, further prevent slipping.

Informed consent as an educational process

Consent should inform the patient in terms she can understand and review all the relevant information a reasonable patient would want in order to make decisions about the planned procedure — not merely enumerate risks.

Port placement, manipulator choice and the order of the dissection are the three decisions that determine how the rest of the operation goes.

Step walkthrough

The laparoscopic hysterectomy, step by step

Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 1 of 9 · Access

Port placement

The camera port is almost always midline, with operative access ports placed laterally.

  • For TLH and LSH with a uterus of 14 weeks or less, the camera port goes midline at the level of the umbilicus.
  • Entry may be closed, optical, open (Hasson) or left upper quadrant (Palmer point). The Hasson method has been associated with decreased vascular injury.
  • For a uterus near or beyond the umbilicus, displace the whole port array superiorly.
Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 2 of 9 · Manipulation

Choosing the manipulator

Choice depends on the procedure, uterine size and occasionally patient size. The larger the uterus, the less any manipulator truly manipulates, and the more work falls to instruments through the accessory ports.

  • LSH — fornix delineation and maintaining pneumoperitoneum are not primary concerns; a Hulka tenaculum or Valtchev manipulator is usually adequate.
  • TLH — both are critical. The colpotomy ring lateralises and protects the ureters and identifies the fornices.
  • A pneumo-occluder, built in or added, maintains pneumoperitoneum after colpotomy until the cuff is closed.
Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 3 of 9 · Landmarks

Identify the ureters

Before anything is divided, confirm the landmarks: ureters, uterosacral ligaments, bladder edge and colpotomy ring.

  • The ureter can usually be seen through intact peritoneum, crossing the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the external and internal iliac vessels.
  • It runs across the sidewall below the infundibulopelvic ligament and above the uterosacral ligament.
  • Where it is visible, retroperitoneal dissection at this point adds no benefit and may cause unnecessary bleeding.
  • Keep its position in view for the rest of the dissection rather than skeletonizing it.

In distorted anatomy, revert to the traditional sequence: incise the round ligament, enter the retroperitoneum, identify the ureter and follow it toward the uterine artery before isolating the adnexa.

Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 4 of 9 · Component 1

Separating the adnexa

Begin by separating ovaries and tubes from the fundus, whether or not they are being removed.

  • The adnexa then stop dangling from the corpus and obscuring access during vessel control, amputation or colpotomy.
  • Any adnexal procedure can be deferred until the uterus is out, giving unencumbered sidewall access from both directions.
  • Proximal tube and utero-ovarian ligament are best transected from the contralateral approach; the round ligament from the ipsilateral approach.
  • With a large or fibroid-distorted uterus, push the uterus medially through one ipsilateral port and dissect through the other.
Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 5 of 9 · Component 2

Creation of the bladder flap

Once the round ligament is transected, the anterior and posterior leaves of the broad ligament separate easily and dissection continues in this avascular plane toward the junction of cervix and corpus.

  • Transecting the anterior leaf across the cervix develops the bladder flap (A).
  • Use cold sharp dissection — or only very brief pulses of bipolar current for superficial peritoneal vessels — until the anatomic limits of the bladder are defined.
  • Tease the loose areolar tissue between the leaves away bluntly or sharply to expose and skeletonize the ascending uterine vessels on the lateral aspect of the uterus (B).
  • Careful skeletonization allows selective vessel sealing, with minimal collateral thermal or mechanical damage.

These steps are identical to their abdominal hysterectomy counterparts.

Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 6 of 9 · Component 2

Uterine vessels, and where to divide them

Retraction from the contralateral side is preferred, since it lets the surgeon use two operative instruments efficiently. Take care not to twist the uterus — it distorts the anatomy and disorients.

  • LSH — coagulate and transect at the junction of the lower uterine segment with the cervix, identifiable in most uteri where the fundal curvature flattens onto the isthmus. Coagulate just inferior to the intended amputation plane.
  • TLH — the skeletonized ascending branches are identified crossing the colpotomy ring, and divided at that level.
  • Coagulating in an ascending manner up the lateral edge decreases back bleeding.
Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 7 of 9 · Component 3

Colpotomy and amputation

The most critical steps of the operation. Whether the anterior or posterior incision comes first does not matter — choose whichever is most identifiable and accessible.

  • A thin monopolar hook electrode on continuous (cutting) current, using the ring as a backstop, delivers focused low-voltage energy.
  • Amputation then becomes a matter of following the ring circumferentially.
  • Oozing is handled with short bursts of discontinuous (coagulation) current.
  • This minimises thermal spread, cuff devitalisation over time, and inadvertent injury to bladder or ureter.
Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 8 of 9 · Deferred adnexectomy

Removing the adnexa

With the uterine corpus out of the way there is unobstructed access to the adnexal structures, which is why removal is usually deferred to this point rather than done at step 4.

  • The infundibulopelvic ligament is now easily distinguished from the ureter (A) for safe coagulation and transection (B).
  • Retract the adnexa medially from the ipsilateral side while securing and transecting the pedicle from the contralateral side.
  • That geometry applies the energy source perpendicular to the pedicle, maximising instrument performance and minimising collateral thermal damage.
  • For salpingectomy alone, coagulate and transect the mesosalpinx instead.

The same window is used to treat benign ovarian pathology or address sidewall adhesions and endometriosis, from both ipsilateral and contralateral approaches.

Click the figure to view it full screen
Step 9 of 9 · Components 4 and 5

Extraction and cuff closure

Uterus, cervix and adnexa are usually removed through the vagina before closing the cuff. A pneumo-occluder balloon, a glove containing a laparotomy pad, or a bulb syringe maintains pneumoperitoneum.

  • Suturing proceeds anterior to posterior, incorporating the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments.
  • Both intracorporeal and extracorporeal knot-tying have been described; unidirectional barbed suture removes the knot-tying step, which is the most skill-limiting component.
  • Incorporating the uterosacral ligaments has been shown to reduce vaginal vault prolapse from 25% to 5% after abdominal or vaginal hysterectomy, and is recommended here by extension.
Principle

Laparoscopy is a different access, not a different procedure. All the steps mimic or correlate with their abdominal counterparts; what changes is magnification and the proximity of the visual field to the target.

Before starting

  • Inspect the upper abdomen by turning the camera cephalad.
  • Lyse any adhesions.
  • Move the bowel gently to the upper abdomen until visualisation is adequate.
  • Identify the anatomic landmarks: ureters, uterosacral ligaments, bladder edge and colpotomy ring.
Port sizing and secondary ports
  • At least one port should be 10–12 mm, often the midline one, to allow a 10-mm laparoscope, suture passage, adhesion barriers or specimen bags.
  • Most other ports can be 5 mm, minimising postoperative pain and trocar-site hernia.
  • Primary lower lateral ports go lateral to the rectus sheath to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels, and far enough cranial to the anterior superior iliac spines for an adequate angle into the deep pelvis.
  • A point at least 2 cm cephalad to the anterior superior iliac spine and at least 2 cm lateral to the rectus sheath is a safe starting point.
  • Upper lateral ports matter more as uterine size increases; place them near the level of the camera port, about halfway between midline and the plane of the lower ports.

Ports placed too low on the abdominal wall — often driven by cosmesis rather than function — give an insufficient angle to the ipsilateral deep pelvis and increase the risk of injury to the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves and the superficial circumflex vessels.

Extraction options and the morcellation controversy

Vaginal morcellation is an excellent technique for larger specimens; each surgeon must judge their own skill and the size at which alternatives are needed. Otherwise the tissue can be removed intact through a small laparotomy incision.

The FDA has warned against morcellating uteri containing fibroids, or fibroids alone, because leiomyosarcoma cannot be diagnosed preoperatively. Reviews by AAGL and ACOG support that morcellation can be performed safely by properly trained surgeons in appropriately screened patients, and an AAGL task force suggests the incidence of leiomyosarcoma was dramatically overestimated, was not age-stratified, and did not weigh the consequences of leiomyosarcoma whether morcellated or not.

Morcellation should not be used where a malignant or premalignant diagnosis is known or suspected — the tissue must come out intact, even if that means a laparotomy incision for the purpose. Contained systems place the specimen in a tear-resistant bag first, with the opening pulled through a slightly enlarged port incision or a purpose-designed trocar; at least one such system has FDA approval.

Amputating too low on the cervix

Many surgeons amputate the fundus too low, either from difficulty judging the plane or from a belief that excising more cervix reduces cyclic bleeding. Post-LSH cyclic bleeding does not appear related to the length of cervix left. Taking too much cervix causes increased bleeding from the rich supply to cervix and upper vagina, and applying electrosurgical energy there risks thermal injury to the ureter or compromise of the cervical stump's blood supply — neither likely to be recognised until days later, presenting as fistula or stump necrosis. Elevate the stump out of the pelvis with a sponge stick and apply energy sparingly, or use clips or sutures instead.

Fulgurating the endocervical canal after amputation seems intuitive but has no evidence behind it; bleeding relates more to patient age and preexisting endometriosis.

Complications after TLH resemble those of abdominal and vaginal hysterectomy, with two additions that are specific to this access: the cuff and the trocars.

Principle

The role of surgeon experience cannot be overstated. Multiple studies show complication rates that plateau after about 100 cases, and lower rates among high-volume laparoscopic surgeons.

Cuff dehiscence

  • Early examination showed a statistically increased incidence with TLH — as high as almost 5%.
  • Two contributing factors: magnification leading the surgeon to believe more tissue is in the suture than really is, and progressive devitalisation of tissue over time from thermal effect during colpotomy, possibly reaching or passing the suture line.
Table 24.1 — Optimal cuff closure
Obtain hemostasis
Approximate tissue without strangulating
Apply minimal amount of thermal energy necessary
Incorporate adequate healthy tissue

Adding a double-layer closure using continuous suturing to these measures has significantly decreased the incidence.

When it dehisces
  • May be partial or complete, with or without bowel evisceration.
  • Without evisceration, revision and reclosure can be done vaginally; laparoscopy or laparotomy is appropriate where bowel or bladder damage is detected or suspected.
  • Expectant management of focal dehiscence is possible, but surgical repair is generally prudent since it may be an area of further separation.
  • Remove all devitalised tissue non-thermally — scissors or scalpel — before reclosure, then close with delayed absorbable suture using 1-cm tissue margins incorporating vaginal mucosa and the pubocervical fascial ring.
  • Bowel evisceration risks peritonitis, bowel necrosis and sepsis; prompt intervention is required, traditionally by laparotomy.

Wound and trocar complications

Lower overall

Smaller incisions, less infection

Postoperative wound infection occurs less frequently with a laparoscopic approach because of incision size.

Trocar-specific

Insertion injuries

Abdominal wall vascular or nerve injury, intra-abdominal vascular or intestinal injury.

Trocar-specific

Site hernia

Estimated at under 1% of cases. Close fascia in a layer separate from skin for any site 10 mm or greater.

At the end

Remove under vision

Trocars should be withdrawn under visualisation at the conclusion of the procedure to watch for bleeding.

Urologic injury

0.73%Urinary tract injury in TLH (2014 review)
0.6% / 0.4%Bladder vs ureteral injury
>90%Ureteral injuries from thermal injury at the cardinal ligament
2%Injury rate above which cystoscopy is cost-effective
  • Gynecologic surgery, and hysterectomy specifically, is the most common cause of iatrogenic urinary tract injury.
  • Risk factors for bladder injury: prior cesarean section, pelvic adhesive disease, endometriosis involving the bladder.
  • 75% of bladder injuries found at posthysterectomy cystoscopy were unsuspected.
  • With immediate cystoscopy, 89% of ureteral and 95% of bladder injuries are detected intraoperatively.
  • Without cystoscopy, intraoperative detection falls to 43% of bladder and only 7% of ureteral injuries.
  • Postoperative morbidity is not increased when bladder injuries are recognised and repaired at the time of surgery; intraoperative identification avoids further surgery and loss of renal function.
Key points from the chapter
  • Choice of access and type of hysterectomy should follow the patient's anatomy and pathology.
  • An appropriate uterine manipulator and fornix delineator should be used for TLH to improve ergonomics and decrease complications.
  • Ureters, bladder and other landmarks should be clearly identified; vessels isolated and skeletonized before coagulation.
  • Understand the electrosurgical and mechanical characteristics of energy-based instruments and apply them to minimise undesired thermal effects.
  • Colpotomy and amputation are the most critical steps with respect to urinary tract injury.
Where laparoscopy sits overall

Minimally invasive hysterectomy, whether vaginal or laparoscopic, offers many advantages. Laparoscopy gives superior exposure to the adnexa and upper abdomen and avoids a large abdominal wall incision, reducing the associated risk of infection, postoperative pain and hernia. Regardless of access, hysterectomy remains relatively safe, with mortality estimated between 0.12 and 0.34 per 1000 procedures.

Source: Anderson TL, Alvarez RD. Minimally Invasive Hysterectomy — Laparoscopic and Robotic-Assisted Hysterectomy. In: Te Linde’s Operative Gynecology, Chapter 24.
